text.p: Content with inflation and economic growth, the Bundesbank will reaffirm a "steady hand" monetary policy at its regular summer news conference and council meeting on Thursday, economists predicted.

All 10 economists surveyed by Reuters on Tuesday said the German central bank would keep interest rates unchanged at the meeting and only one expected any move in the discount or Lombard rates any time this year.

"The economy is still so weak, especially domestically, that there is no need to raise rates," said Mathias Haffner, economist at Barclays de Zoete Wedd in Frankfurt. "Lower interest rates would not help the situation either."

The meeting, taking place in the picturesque south German town of Aschau, will be followed by a press conference at which the Bundesbank will elaborate on its view of the economy and progress toward European economic and monetary union.
But economists said that the Bundesbank had little to say, at least on the domestic economy,

The Bundesbank had already made clear there was little room to cut already historically low interest rates and that signs of an economic upturn were still too faint for the central bank to consider raising rates, they said.
Last Friday, Bundesbank Chief Economist Otmar Issing said that all the pieces were in place for the economy to recover but that there was no need to lower rates.

"As far as foreign exchange rates, the price situation and unit wage costs go, everything is in place for the upturn to continue and strengthen," he said, adding: "Interest rate cuts would be absolutely counterproductive."
About the only problem the Bundesbank must watch is the weakness of the mark, now trading above 1.76 to the dollar.
Germany historically has suffered under a strong U.S. currency which can lead to "imported inflation" where more marks are required to buy dollar-denominated imports such as oil.

Although Bundesbank council members have the power at least to blunt the dollar's advance by expressing a desire for the mark to reclaim lost ground, they have so far been quiet about developments on the foreign exchange market.
Economists said that although import price inflation could pick up, increases so far have been offset by declining unit wage costs.

"The D-mark is soft, there are no inflation pressures, so (there is) no need for a cut or a rise (in interest rates). They are going to have some beer and sandwiches at this nice Bavarian lake," said Steven King, economist at James Capel in London.

The Bundesbank has been a focal point in much of the recent debate about monetary union, but Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer, the featured speaker at the press conference, is unlikely to go beyond recent statements on the project.

Tietmeyer has avoided sticking his neck out on the likelihood of EMU, traditionally saying he hopes Germany can meet Maastricht Treaty deficit criteria and that sustained fiscal stability should determine which nations are allowed to start the project.

None of the economists contacted by Reuters expected the central bank to move on rates this Thursday. But they will be reading between the lines for any hint about the central bank's long-term views on the economy when some believe it may raise rates.

"Until the second quarter of 1998 the Bundesbank won't change anything. First there will be small increments in the repo...Then in the third quarter the discount and Lombard will follow," said Sonja Gibbs, economist at Nomura International in London.
